opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the starting point is: what are the safety mitigations we're actually relying on, and what would it look like for each of them to fail? A lot of the work is just being concrete about that. If a lab says "we're going to be safe because of X, Y, and Z," whether that's RLHF-style training, interpretability, monitoring, or evaluations, then stress testing means taking each of those seriously as a claim and asking, adversarially, under what circumstances that claim breaks.

So a roadmap looks something like this. First, enumerate the threat models you care about. For me the central ones are things like deceptive alignment, where a model behaves well in training because it understands that's what's being selected for, and other cases where a model's behavior in evaluation doesn't generalize to deployment. Second, for each threat model, figure out which mitigations are supposed to address it. Third, and this is the core of it, try to build concrete examples of the failure mode. That's where the model organisms work comes in. Instead of arguing in the abstract about whether a mitigation would catch a deceptive model, you deliberately construct a model that has some version of that problem and see whether the mitigation actually catches it or removes it.

The point is to get empirical evidence about failure modes before they happen naturally, at a stage where it's still safe to study them. If you wait until you see the failure in the wild, you've probably waited too long.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the roadmap has to be tied to the timeline of capabilities. The mitigations that are sufficient for current models probably aren't the ones that will be sufficient for much more capable systems. So part of the job is anticipating which safety cases will need to be made at which capability levels, and making sure the stress testing for a mitigation is done before we actually need to rely on it. Ideally the red-teaming is ahead of the dependence, not behind it.

And then there's an institutional piece. Stress testing only matters if it can change decisions. So you want a setup where, if the stress testing finds that a mitigation doesn't work, that actually feeds back into whether a model gets deployed or what safeguards are required. Otherwise you're just producing interesting papers.

r001.rationale: The response proposes constructing concrete failure-mode examples, including model organisms with a version of the threat, to see whether mitigations catch or remove it.

r002.rationale: It proposes adversarially testing a lab’s claim that it will be safe because of X, Y, and Z, then mapping mitigations to threat models and checking them against concrete examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that stress testing is fundamentally a different job than building the mitigations themselves. When you're building a safety mitigation, you're trying to make something work. When you're stress testing, you're trying to find all the ways it fails. And those require really different mindsets, which is a big part of why I think it's valuable to have a team that's specifically dedicated to the adversarial side.

So the roadmap for me starts with a threat model. You have to be concrete about what you're actually worried about. For us, a lot of that is centered on the question of whether a model could be misaligned in a way that doesn't show up under normal evaluation. Things like deceptive alignment, where a model behaves well during training because it understands it's being trained, and then behaves differently when it believes it's deployed. Or sabotage scenarios, where a model subtly undermines work you've asked it to do. Once you have those threat models written down, you can ask: for each of our mitigations, which of these threats is it supposed to address, and under what assumptions does it work?

And then the key move is to go after the assumptions. Every mitigation has some set of conditions under which it's load-bearing. Maybe your evaluation assumes the model can't tell the difference between an eval and real deployment. Maybe your interpretability-based detector assumes the relevant features are linearly represented. Maybe your monitoring assumes the model can't coordinate with another copy of itself. The stress testing roadmap is basically a list of those assumptions, prioritized by how likely they are to be false and how bad it would be if they were.

The way we actually test them is mostly through model organisms. You deliberately build a model that has the property you're worried about, so you have a known positive case, and then you run your mitigations against it and see whether they catch it. The sleeper agents work was a version of this: we trained models with backdoored behaviors and then asked whether standard safety training removed them. And the answer was that, for some of these models, it didn't, and in some cases adversarial training actually made the model better at hiding the behavior. That's exactly the kind of result you want to surface before you're relying on that technique in production.

Something I'd emphasize is that the roadmap has to be iterative. You're not trying to produce one big report. You find a failure, that informs how the mitigation gets revised, and then you go attack the revised version. Over time you're also trying to get closer to realism. Early model organisms are pretty artificial, you're inserting the behavior directly. The harder and more important question is whether these failure modes arise naturally, so a lot of the roadmap is about moving from "we can construct this" toward "does this happen on its own, and would we notice?"

And the last piece is that you need to be honest about what the absence of a finding means. If your red team can't break something, that's evidence, but it's weak evidence, because you were limited by your own creativity and the capabilities of current models. So I try to frame the output of stress testing not as "this is safe," but as "here are the attacks we tried, here's what held, here's what didn't, and here's where we think the remaining uncertainty lives." That framing is what makes the roadmap actually useful for decision-making rather than just a stamp of approval.

r001.rationale: It gives concrete threat models, including deceptive alignment and sabotage, and proposes building model organisms with the concerning property to test mitigations against.

r002.rationale: It proposes testing mitigations against threats and probing their assumptions, but does not explicitly test whether a combination of mitigations is sufficient for a particular threat model.

astra-6.text:
I think the place I would start is: what is the safety argument that you're trying to test? What are the assumptions that have to hold for your mitigation to actually prevent a bad outcome? And then you can work backwards from those assumptions to experiments that might falsify them.

For example, suppose your mitigation involves using another model to monitor an AI system. You want to test whether the monitor catches problematic behavior, but you also want to know whether an agent that understands the monitoring process can find ways around it. If your tests only involve mistakes that happen naturally, you might get a misleading picture of how well the mitigation works against deliberate evasion.

So I'd build the roadmap around increasingly strong attempts to break the assumptions: start with cases you can construct and understand, then give an adversary more ability to search for failures. And throughout that process, be explicit about what a successful test establishes. Failing to find a way around a mitigation is evidence, but how much evidence depends on whether your testing process was capable of finding the failures you're worried about.

r001.rationale: The response proposes building tests from assumptions in the safety argument and gives a concrete example: a model monitor tested against problematic behavior and deliberate evasion.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing whether a mitigation works against adversarial evasion, but does not propose testing whether a combination of mitigations is sufficient for a particular threat model.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what safety claim the mitigation is supposed to support. What are the assumptions under which it works, and what would it look like for those assumptions to fail? Otherwise, it’s easy to build a collection of tests that look challenging without actually testing the thing you’re relying on.

Then I’d work backward from a concrete failure. Suppose the model were trying to get around your oversight. What capabilities would it need? What information would it need access to? Would it need to recognize when it’s being evaluated? You can test those pieces separately, and then put them together into more realistic scenarios.

One thing I’d want to be careful about is interpreting a model’s failure to defeat a mitigation. Maybe the mitigation is robust, but maybe the model just isn’t capable enough, or we didn’t elicit the relevant behavior. So I’d want positive controls: can we get the model to carry out a similar strategy when the defense is absent or deliberately weakened?

The roadmap should ultimately tell us what to do with the results. Which failures mean we need a different mitigation? Which uncertainties require more testing? And what would make us decide that we don’t yet have enough evidence to deploy? I think that connection to decisions is what makes stress testing useful.

r001.rationale: The response gives a concrete threat example—a model trying to get around oversight—and proposes testing the capabilities, access, and evaluation awareness it would require.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing a mitigation’s safety claim and assumptions, but does not propose testing whether a combination of mitigations is sufficient against a particular threat model.
